claim: Malaria remains a serious health burden globally, with over 216 million cases annually.
source: Malaria remains a serious health burden globally, with over 216 million cases annually (WHO, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to WHO, 2018.

claim: Plasmodium falciparum is responsible for 99% of estimated malaria cases in sub-Saharan Africa.
source: Plasmodium falciparum is responsible for 99% of estimated malaria cases in sub-Saharan Africa.
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction section and is part of established scientific knowledge about malaria epidemiology.

claim: P. vivax causes approximately 7.4 million clinical cases annually outside Africa.
source: Outside Africa, P. vivax is the predominant parasite and causes ~ 7.4 million clinical cases annually.
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and represents epidemiological data.

claim: In 2016 the number of malaria cases were on the rise again for the first time in several years.
source: Despite extensive efforts, in 2016 the number of malaria cases were on the rise again for the first time in several years (WHO, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to WHO, 2018.

claim: P. vivax and P. knowlesi are closely related and occupy a separate simian parasite clade to P. falciparum.
source: Although P. vivax displays some distinctive features to P. knowlesi, including the formation of latent hypnozoites stages in the liver and restriction to reticulocytes in the blood, the two parasites are closely related, occupying a separate simian parasite clade to P. falciparum (Pacheco et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pacheco et al., 2018.

claim: Host cell invasion by P. vivax and P. knowlesi relies on the Duffy binding proteins (DBP) PvDBP and PkDBPα, respectively.
source: Host cell invasion by P. vivax and P. knowlesi relies on the Duffy binding proteins (DBP) PvDBP and PkDBPα, respectively, both ligands for human red blood cell (RBC) Duffy antigen/receptor for chemokines (DARC) (Adams et al., 1990; Horuk et al., 1993; Singh et al., 2005; Miller et al., 1975).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations: Adams et al., 1990; Horuk et al., 1993; Singh et al., 2005; Miller et al., 1975.

claim: PvDBP and PkDBPα are ligands for human red blood cell Duffy antigen/receptor for chemokines (DARC).
source: Host cell invasion by P. vivax and P. knowlesi relies on the Duffy binding proteins (DBP) PvDBP and PkDBPα, respectively, both ligands for human red blood cell (RBC) Duffy antigen/receptor for chemokines (DARC) (Adams et al., 1990; Horuk et al., 1993; Singh et al., 2005; Miller et al., 1975).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations: Adams et al., 1990; Horuk et al., 1993; Singh et al., 2005; Miller et al., 1975.

claim: The critical binding motif of the DBP ligands is the cysteine-rich region 2 (DBP-RII).
source: The critical binding motif of the ligands is the cysteine-rich region 2 (DBP-RII) (Chitnis and Miller, 1994), with ~70% identity between PkDBPα and PvDBP (Ranjan and Chitnis, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chitnis and Miller, 1994.

claim: PkDBPα and PvDBP have approximately 70% identity.
source: The critical binding motif of the ligands is the cysteine-rich region 2 (DBP-RII) (Chitnis and Miller, 1994), with ~70% identity between PkDBPα and PvDBP (Ranjan and Chitnis, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ranjan and Chitnis, 1999.

claim: PvDBP has been implicated in P. vivax reticulocyte restriction.
source: Despite their similarity, PvDBP has also been implicated in both P. vivax reticulocyte restriction (Ovchynnikova et al., 2017) and as a host tropism factor preventing P. vivax from infecting macaques (Tachibana et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ovchynnikova et al., 2017.

claim: PvDBP has been implicated as a host tropism factor preventing P. vivax from infecting macaques.
source: Despite their similarity, PvDBP has also been implicated in both P. vivax reticulocyte restriction (Ovchynnikova et al., 2017) and as a host tropism factor preventing P. vivax from infecting macaques (Tachibana et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tachibana et al., 2015.

claim: PvDBP-RII is the leading blood stage vaccine candidate for P. vivax.
source: PvDBP-RII is also the leading blood stage vaccine candidate for P. vivax (Ntumngia et al., 2012; Payne et al., 2017a; Singh et al., 2018), with antibodies targeting PvDBP-RII blocking parasite invasion in ex vivo P. vivax assays (Russell et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations: Ntumngia et al., 2012; Payne et al., 2017a; Singh et al., 2018.

claim: Antibodies targeting PvDBP-RII block parasite invasion in ex vivo P. vivax assays.
source: PvDBP-RII is also the leading blood stage vaccine candidate for P. vivax (Ntumngia et al., 2012; Payne et al., 2017a; Singh et al., 2018), with antibodies targeting PvDBP-RII blocking parasite invasion in ex vivo P. vivax assays (Russell et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Russell et al., 2011.

claim: P. knowlesi contains two PkDBPα paralogues, DBPβ and DBPγ.
source: P. knowlesi additionally contains two PkDBPα paralogues, namely DBPβ and DBPγ which share high levels of amino acid identity (68–88%) to PkDBPα but bind to distinct receptors via N-glycolylneuraminic acid - a sialic acid found on the surface of macaque RBCs, but absent from human RBCs (Dankwa et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Dankwa et al., 2016.

claim: DBPβ and DBPγ share 68–88% amino acid identity to PkDBPα.
source: P. knowlesi additionally contains two PkDBPα paralogues, namely DBPβ and DBPγ which share high levels of amino acid identity (68–88%) to PkDBPα but bind to distinct receptors via N-glycolylneuraminic acid - a sialic acid found on the surface of macaque RBCs, but absent from human RBCs (Dankwa et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dankwa et al., 2016.

claim: DBPβ and DBPγ bind to distinct receptors via N-glycolylneuraminic acid, a sialic acid found on macaque RBCs but absent from human RBCs.
source: P. knowlesi additionally contains two PkDBPα paralogues, namely DBPβ and DBPγ which share high levels of amino acid identity (68–88%) to PkDBPα but bind to distinct receptors via N-glycolylneuraminic acid - a sialic acid found on the surface of macaque RBCs, but absent from human RBCs (Dankwa et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dankwa et al., 2016.

claim: P. knowlesi has been adapted to long-term culture in human RBCs.
source: The evolutionary similarity between P. vivax and P. knowlesi means the adaptation of P. knowlesi to long-term culture in human RBCs (Moon et al., 2013; Lim et al., 2013) provides unique opportunities to study DARC-dependent invasion processes in both species.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Moon et al., 2013 and Lim et al., 2013.

claim: CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing has been adapted to P. falciparum.
source: While adaptation of the CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing system to the most prevalent malaria parasite, P. falciparum (Ghorbal et al., 2014), provided a powerful tool for studying parasite biology, scalable approaches for P. falciparum remain constrained by inefficient transfection and very high genome AT-content (averaging 80.6%) (Gardner et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ghorbal et al., 2014.

claim: P. falciparum has a genome AT-content averaging 80.6%.
source: While adaptation of the CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing system to the most prevalent malaria parasite, P. falciparum (Ghorbal et al., 2014), provided a powerful tool for studying parasite biology, scalable approaches for P. falciparum remain constrained by inefficient transfection and very high genome AT-content (averaging 80.6%) (Gardner et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gardner et al., 2002.

claim: P. knowlesi has a genome AT-content of 62.5%.
source: P. knowlesi offers significant experimental advantages over P. falciparum including a more balanced genome AT-content of 62.5% and orders-of-magnitude-more-efficient transgenesis (Moon et al., 2013; Grüring et al., 2014; Kocken et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: P. knowlesi has orders-of-magnitude-more-efficient transgenesis compared to P. falciparum.
source: P. knowlesi offers significant experimental advantages over P. falciparum including a more balanced genome AT-content of 62.5% and orders-of-magnitude-more-efficient transgenesis (Moon et al., 2013; Grüring et al., 2014; Kocken et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Moon et al., 2013; Grüring et al., 2014; Kocken et al., 2002.

claim: CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing was established in P. knowlesi.
source: Here, we establish CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing in P. knowlesi.
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and is a primary finding of the study.

claim: A scalable PCR-based protocol for the production of repair templates was established.
source: We establish a scalable protocol for the production of repair templates by PCR and demonstrate the flexibility of the system by tagging proteins with distinct cellular localisations.
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and is a primary finding of the study.

claim: A transgenic P. knowlesi line expressing P. vivax Duffy binding protein (PvDBP) was generated using iterative genome-editing.
source: Using iterative rounds of genome-editing we generate a transgenic line expressing P. vivax Duffy binding protein (PvDBP), a lead vaccine candidate.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is a primary finding of the study.

claim: PvDBP plays no role in reticulocyte restriction.
source: We demonstrate that PvDBP plays no role in reticulocyte restriction but can alter the macaque/human host cell tropism of P. knowlesi.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: PvDBP can alter the macaque/human host cell tropism of P. knowlesi.
source: We demonstrate that PvDBP plays no role in reticulocyte restriction but can alter the macaque/human host cell tropism of P. knowlesi.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Antibodies raised against PvDBP potently inhibit proliferation of the PvDBP-expressing P. knowlesi strain.
source: Critically, antibodies raised against the P. vivax antigen potently inhibit proliferation of this strain, providing an invaluable tool to support vaccine development.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Plasmodium parasites lack a canonical non-homologous end joining pathway.
source: Plasmodium parasites lack a canonical non-homologous end joining pathway, instead relying almost exclusively on homology-directed repair of double-stranded breaks (DSBs), such as those introduced by the Cas9 endonuclease.
evidence: The claim is stated in the results section and represents established knowledge about Plasmodium DNA repair mechanisms.

claim: Plasmodium parasites rely almost exclusively on homology-directed repair of double-stranded breaks.
source: Plasmodium parasites lack a canonical non-homologous end joining pathway, instead relying almost exclusively on homology-directed repair of double-stranded breaks (DSBs), such as those introduced by the Cas9 endonuclease.
evidence: The claim is stated in the results section and represents established knowledge about Plasmodium DNA repair mechanisms.

claim: Transfection efficiency is significantly higher in P. knowlesi than P. falciparum.
source: As transfection efficiency is significantly higher in P. knowlesi than P. falciparum (Grüring et al., 2014), we reasoned that we may be able to use a single positive drug selectable marker to cover all the required components for editing.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Grüring et al., 2014.

claim: Approximately 30% of P. knowlesi transgenic parasites took up both co-transfected plasmids expressing eGFP and mCherry.
source: Supporting this approach, co-transfection of plasmids expressing eGFP or mCherry revealed that ~30% of P. knowlesi transgenic parasites took up both plasmids, although the proportion expressing both declined rapidly in the following days (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The proportion of P. knowlesi parasites expressing both eGFP and mCherry declined rapidly in the days following co-transfection.
source: Supporting this approach, co-transfection of plasmids expressing eGFP or mCherry revealed that ~30% of P. knowlesi transgenic parasites took up both plasmids, although the proportion expressing both declined rapidly in the following days (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Correct integration of eGFP at the p230p locus was detectable by PCR within 3 days of transfection.
source: Correct integration at the p230p locus was detectable by PCR within 3 days of transfection and only low levels of wild type DNA was detectable after day 11 (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Only low levels of wild type DNA was detectable after day 11 post-transfection.
source: Correct integration at the p230p locus was detectable by PCR within 3 days of transfection and only low levels of wild type DNA was detectable after day 11 (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The transfection efficiency for the p230p eGFP integration was 8.4%±2.1 SD.
source: The eGFP positivity rate was calculated the day after transfection (day 1), to evaluate transfection efficiency (8.4%±2.1 SD).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: 83.3% (±1.8 SD) of parasites had integrated the eGFP construct by day 12 when parasites reached 0.5% parasitemia.
source: The eGFP positivity was assessed again once parasites reached 0.5% parasitemia (day 12), indicating 83.3% (±1.8 SD) of the parasites had integrated the construct (Figure 1D); Figure 1—source data 1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Parasites transfected with pCas9/sg_p230p without pDonor_p230p retained an intact guide and PAM site.
source: Parasites transfected with pCas9/sg_p230p without providing pDonor_p230p were visible in culture several days after the integrated lines. An intact guide and PAM site was detected in these parasites, suggesting that a small population of parasites did not form DSB.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from the study.

claim: Cas9 expression without a targeting sgRNA is not toxic to P. knowlesi parasites.
source: Parasites transfected with pCas9/sg without a cloned sgRNA appeared in culture within a few days after transfection, with comparable growth rates to the eGFP plasmid, suggesting the Cas9 expression without a targeting sgRNA is not toxic (Figure 1E); Figure 1—source data 1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 10/10 genotyped clones harboured correctly integrated, markerless eGFP.
source: Clones were identified using a plaque-based assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) previously used for P. falciparum (Thomas et al., 2016), and 10/10 genotyped clone's harboured correctly integrated, markerless eGFP (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: P. knowlesi readily accepts linearised plasmids for homologous recombination.
source: P. knowlesi readily accepts linearised plasmids for homologous recombination (Moon et al., 2013; Kocken et al., 2002; Moon et al., 2016), so we next tested whether we could use a PCR-based approach for scalable generation of repair templates.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Moon et al., 2013; Kocken et al., 2002; Moon et al., 2016.

claim: A three-step PCR scheme was developed to generate repair templates by fusing homology regions with the desired insertion.
source: Modifying a method used for homologous recombination in P. berghei (Ecker et al., 2006), we developed a three-step PCR scheme which first amplified the eGFP cassette and 400 bp HRs with eGFP cassette adaptors separately, with the second and third reactions fusing each HR to the eGFP cassette in turn (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the method and Figure 2A.

claim: PCR repair templates with 400 bp HRs resulted in 74% (±8 SD) eGFP positivity, similar to plasmid-based repair templates.
source: The final PCR construct (HR1-eGFPcassette-HR2) was transfected along with the pCas9/sg_p230p plasmid (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), and resultant parasite lines demonstrated integration by PCR (Figure 2B), and an eGFP positivity rate of 74% (±8 SD), similar to that seen for the pDonor_p230p plasmid (Figure 2C); Figure 2—source data 1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The use of a high-fidelity, high-processivity polymerase allowed each PCR reaction to be completed in 40–90 min.
source: The use of a high-fidelity, high-processivity polymerase for the construct production allowed each reaction to be completed in 40–90 min, thus providing a rapid method for generating repair templates.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from the study.

claim: Increasing HR length enhanced integration efficiency proportionately in P. knowlesi.
source: We systematically tested key parameters associated with successful genome editing and found increasing HR length enhanced integration efficiency proportionately, a trend seen in both P. falciparum and P. berghei (Collins et al., 2013; Wagner et al., 2014; MacPherson and Scherf, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study and citations to similar findings in other Plasmodium species.

claim: Integration was detected with HRs as short as 50 bp.
source: Whilst integration was detected with HRs as short as 50 bp, efficient editing was achieved with HRs between 200–800 bp.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Efficient editing was achieved with HRs between 200–800 bp.
source: Whilst integration was detected with HRs as short as 50 bp, efficient editing was achieved with HRs between 200–800 bp.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Parasites transfected with 800 and 1600 bp HR constructs reached 1% parasitemia on day 12 and 9 post transfection, respectively.
source: Parasites transfected with 800 and 1600 bp HR constructs were the fastest to reach 1% parasitemia on day 12 and 9 post transfection, respectively (Figure 2E); Figure 2—source data 1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Constructs with HRs > 400 bp provided GFP positivity ranging from 79% and 81%.
source: Constructs with HRs > 400 bp provided GFP positivity ranging from 79% and 81% (Figure 2F); Figure 2—source data 1, which taken together with PCR yields and transfection recovery time suggest an optimal HR length of at least ~800 bp.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The optimal HR length for P. knowlesi genome editing is at least ~800 bp.
source: Constructs with HRs > 400 bp provided GFP positivity ranging from 79% and 81% (Figure 2F); Figure 2—source data 1, which taken together with PCR yields and transfection recovery time suggest an optimal HR length of at least ~800 bp.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental observations including GFP positivity, PCR yields, and transfection recovery time.

claim: Integration efficiency declined with distance from the Cas9-induced DSB.
source: Whilst all transfections were PCR positive for integration and reached 1% parasitemia at similar times (14–20 days) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, Figure 2H and Figure 2—source data 1), the integration efficiency declined with distance from DSB.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: HRs placed 5 kb away from the DSB yielded a 14% (±18 SD) integration efficiency.
source: This decline was surprisingly small, with HRs placed even 5 kb away from either side of the DSB yielding a 14% (±18 SD) integration efficiency (Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Extending HR length to 800 bp restored integration efficiencies to 54.8% (±8.7 SD) at a 5 kb distance from DSB.
source: Interestingly, we found that extending HR length to 800 bp restored integration efficiencies to 54.8% (±8.7 SD) at a 5 kb distance from DSB (Figure 2I; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: HR length can directly offset efficiency losses due to distance from DSB.
source: Thus, HR length can directly offset efficiency losses due to distance from DSB and this system can readily remove genes at least as large as 10 kb in size from a single PAM site, accounting for ~98% of genes in the P. knowlesi genome (Pain et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing that longer HRs restore integration efficiency at greater distances from DSB.

claim: This CRISPR-Cas9 system can readily remove genes at least as large as 10 kb in size from a single PAM site.
source: Thus, HR length can directly offset efficiency losses due to distance from DSB and this system can readily remove genes at least as large as 10 kb in size from a single PAM site, accounting for ~98% of genes in the P. knowlesi genome (Pain et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data and is supported by a citation to Pain et al., 2008 regarding P. knowlesi genome composition.

claim: The CRISPR-Cas9 system can target ~98% of genes in the P. knowlesi genome.
source: Thus, HR length can directly offset efficiency losses due to distance from DSB and this system can readily remove genes at least as large as 10 kb in size from a single PAM site, accounting for ~98% of genes in the P. knowlesi genome (Pain et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the ability to delete 10 kb genes and is supported by a citation to Pain et al., 2008.

claim: Five genes with disparate subcellular locations and functions were successfully tagged using the PCR-based CRISPR-Cas9 approach.
source: We selected five genes with disparate subcellular locations and functions to test this approach: the micronemal protein apical membrane antigen 1 (AMA1) (Bannister et al., 2003), rhoptry neck protein 2 (RON2) (Cao et al., 2009), inner membrane complex protein myosin A (MyoA) (Baum et al., 2006), digestive vacuole membrane protein involved in drug resistance CRT (Ehlgen et al., 2012), and a protein involved in artemisinin resistance in cytoplasmic foci Kelch13 (K13) (Birnbaum et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing successful tagging of these proteins.

claim: All tagged parasite lines grew up quickly after transfection, reaching 1% parasitemia between 8 and 15 days.
source: All lines grew up quickly after transfection, reaching 1% after between 8 and 15 days, and PCR analysis indicated that correct integration had occurred (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: All tagged proteins demonstrated localisation patterns consistent with previous reports for P. falciparum.
source: Whilst it is, to our knowledge, the first time each of these proteins have been tagged in P. knowlesi, all demonstrated localisation patterns were consistent with previous reports for P. falciparum (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and comparison to previous literature.

claim: CRT-eGFP fusion protein migrates at ~50 kDa, faster than its predicted size of 76 kDa.
source: The CRT-eGFP fusion protein showed a band at ~50 kDa, in line with work in P. falciparum which showed CRT-eGFP migrates faster than its predicted size of 76 kDa (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F) (Ehlgen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and a citation to Ehlgen et al., 2012.

claim: Only 2/5 equivalent P. falciparum loci had suitably positioned PAM sites for the same tagging approach.
source: Analysis of equivalent P. falciparum loci revealed only 2/5 had suitably positioned PAM sites, and equivalent UTR regions had an average GC-content of only 11.8% (36% for P. knowlesi), suggesting a similar approach would have been more challenging in P. falciparum (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Equivalent UTR regions in P. falciparum had an average GC-content of only 11.8% compared to 36% for P. knowlesi.
source: Analysis of equivalent P. falciparum loci revealed only 2/5 had suitably positioned PAM sites, and equivalent UTR regions had an average GC-content of only 11.8% (36% for P. knowlesi), suggesting a similar approach would have been more challenging in P. falciparum (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: PkDBPα and PvDBP are orthologous RBC ligands that mediate host cell invasion by binding to the DARC receptor.
source: The orthologous RBC ligands PkDBPα and PvDBP, mediate host cell invasion by binding to the DARC receptor on human RBCs in P. knowlesi and P. vivax, respectively (Adams et al., 1990; Horuk et al., 1993; Singh et al., 2005; Miller et al., 1975).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Adams et al., 1990; Horuk et al., 1993; Singh et al., 2005; Miller et al., 1975.

claim: The DBP orthologues PkDBPα and PvDBP are antigenically distinct with ~70% amino acid identity in binding region II.
source: Whilst likely functionally equivalent, the DBP orthologues are antigenically distinct (~70% amino acid identity in binding region II) so we used genome-editing to generate transgenic P. knowlesi parasites in which DARC binding is provided solely by PvDBP.
evidence: The claim is stated in the results section and represents established knowledge.

claim: Successful orthologue replacement of PkDBPα with PvDBP was achieved in P. knowlesi.
source: We first carried out an orthologue replacement (OR) of the full-length PkDBPα with PvDBP in the P. knowlesi A1-H.1 line (PvDBPOR) – using a recodonised synthetic PvDBP gene flanked by HRs targeting the 5' and 3'UTRs of the PkDBPα gene (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A). Once integrated, this deletes the PkDBPα gene and places the PvDBP gene under control of the PkDBPα regulatory sequences, enabling a precisely matched expression profile. As a control we also exchanged PkDBPα with a recodonised PkDBPα gene (PkDBPαOR) using the same sgRNA. Successful integration was readily achieved and limiting dilution cloning resulted in 100% integrated clones for PkDBPαOR and 40% for PvDBPOR (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Limiting dilution cloning resulted in 100% integrated clones for PkDBPαOR and 40% for PvDBPOR.
source: Successful integration was readily achieved and limiting dilution cloning resulted in 100% integrated clones for PkDBPαOR and 40% for PvDBPOR (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The PkA1-H.1 line relies on the DARC receptor for invasion of human RBCs.
source: The PkA1-H.1 line relies on the DARC receptor for invasion of human RBCs (Moon et al., 2013) and PkDBPα is required to mediate this interaction (Singh et al., 2005), thus the successful replacement indicates that the Pv orthologue can complement its role in DARC binding sufficiently well to maintain growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Moon et al., 2013.

claim: PkDBPα is required to mediate DARC-dependent invasion in P. knowlesi.
source: The PkA1-H.1 line relies on the DARC receptor for invasion of human RBCs (Moon et al., 2013) and PkDBPα is required to mediate this interaction (Singh et al., 2005), thus the successful replacement indicates that the Pv orthologue can complement its role in DARC binding sufficiently well to maintain growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Singh et al., 2005.

claim: PvDBP can complement the role of PkDBPα in DARC binding sufficiently well to maintain growth.
source: The PkA1-H.1 line relies on the DARC receptor for invasion of human RBCs (Moon et al., 2013) and PkDBPα is required to mediate this interaction (Singh et al., 2005), thus the successful replacement indicates that the Pv orthologue can complement its role in DARC binding sufficiently well to maintain growth.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the successful growth of the PvDBPOR line.

claim: The PkDBPαOR and PvDBPOR lines have a ~44 kb truncation at one end of chromosome 14.
source: However, diagnostic PCRs for DBPβ failed, as well as PCRs in genes flanking the DBPβ locus. Whole genome sequencing and mapping against the A1-H.1 reference genome revealed that the PkDBPαOR and PvDBPOR line have a ~ 44 kb truncation at one end of chromosome 14 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), which also harbours DBPβ, therefore we renamed the lines PkDBPαOR/Δ14 and PvDBPOR/Δ14.
evidence: The claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The ~44 kb deletion on chromosome 14 occurred in the A1-H.1 parental parasite line prior to transfection.
source: The loss of the ~44 kb of chromosome 14 is also present in parasites that have been transfected simultaneously with pCas/sg_p230p, suggesting that the 44 kb deletion occurred in the A1-H.1 parental parasite line (wt/Δ14) prior to transfection and was not an artefact caused by targeting DBPα.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that the deletion is present in parasites transfected with a different construct.

claim: The disruption of DBPβ was unlikely to be induced by Cas9 during DBPα targeting because the PAM site of the DBPα targeting guide sequence is absent in DBPβ.
source: Furthermore, the PAM site of the DBPα targeting guide sequence is absent in DBPβ (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) which makes it unlikely that the disruption of DBPβ was induced by Cas9 during DBPα targeting.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the absence of the PAM site in DBPβ as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: No off-target mutations were detected in the four most similar target sequences to the PkDBPα sgRNA in the PvDBPOR lines.
source: We therefore sequenced the four most similar target sequences, including one in DBPγ, in the PvDBPOR lines (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and did not detect any off-target mutations, suggesting that as for other malaria parasites (Ghorbal et al., 2014) the absence of non-homologous end joining ameliorates the potential for off-target mutations.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data and comparison to other malaria parasites.

claim: PkDBPβ and PkDBPγ are dispensable for multiplication in human RBCs.
source: This confirmed that the P. vivax protein was able to complement the role of its P. knowlesi orthologue. It also demonstrated, that not only are PkDBPβ and γ proteins dispensable for multiplication in humans RBCs (Dankwa et al., 2016), but as their loss leads to increased multiplication rate, they may actually impede invasion in human RBCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Dankwa et al., 2016.

claim: Loss of PkDBPβ and PkDBPγ leads to increased multiplication rate in human RBCs.
source: Analysis of the wild type line, and the four transgenic lines (PkDBPαOR/Δ14, PvDBPOR/Δ14, PkDBPαOR/Δ14Δγ and PvDBPOR/Δ14Δγ) revealed no difference in growth rate in human RBCs for all lines except the PkDBPαOR/Δ14Δγ which demonstrated significantly increased growth rate compared to wild type (Figure 4C and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: PkDBPβ and PkDBPγ may impede invasion in human RBCs.
source: It also demonstrated, that not only are PkDBPβ and γ proteins dispensable for multiplication in humans RBCs (Dankwa et al., 2016), but as their loss leads to increased multiplication rate, they may actually impede invasion in human RBCs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that deletion of these genes increases multiplication rate.

claim: The PkDBPαOR/Δ14Δγ line showed significantly higher growth rates (8.9 fold) compared to the wild type line (6.9 fold) and PvDBPOR/Δ14Δγ line in 21 Duffy positive blood donations.
source: A further experiment comparing multiplication rates in 21 Duffy positive blood donations revealed significant higher growth rates of the PkDBPαOR/Δ14Δγ line (8.9 fold) compared to the 6.9 fold multiplication of the wild type line and PvDBPOR/Δ14Δγ line (p<0.001) (Figure 4D and Figure 4—source data 1), confirming that knockout of the two paralogues increases multiplication rate in human RBCs but also revealing a minor growth reduction in the PvDBPOR/Δ14Δγ line compared to its control line.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The PvDBPOR/Δ14Δγ line showed a minor growth reduction compared to the PkDBPαOR/Δ14Δγ control line.
source: A further experiment comparing multiplication rates in 21 Duffy positive blood donations revealed significant higher growth rates of the PkDBPαOR/Δ14Δγ line (8.9 fold) compared to the 6.9 fold multiplication of the wild type line and PvDBPOR/Δ14Δγ line (p<0.001) (Figure 4D and Figure 4—source data 1), confirming that knockout of the two paralogues increases multiplication rate in human RBCs but also revealing a minor growth reduction in the PvDBPOR/Δ14Δγ line compared to its control line.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Loss of DBPβ and DBPγ in the PkDBPαOR/Δ14Δγ line did not reduce the parasite multiplication rate in macaque RBC but rather slightly increased it.
source: Interestingly, loss of DBPβ and DBPγ in the PkDBPαOR/Δ14Δγ line did not reduce the parasite multiplication rate in macaque RBC but rather slightly increased it (Figure 4C), with the lines retaining a macaque preference ratio (macaque fold growth/human fold growth) of 1.43, similar to both the wild type (1.26) and PkDBPαOR/Δ14 (1.33).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: PkDBPβ and PkDBPγ are dispensable for invasion of macaque RBCs.
source: This demonstrates that both PkDBPβ and PkDBPγ are dispensable for invasion of macaque RBCs, and PkDBPα is sufficient to retain full growth rate in macaque cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that deletion of these genes does not reduce growth in macaque RBCs.

claim: PkDBPα is sufficient to retain full growth rate in macaque cells.
source: This demonstrates that both PkDBPβ and PkDBPγ are dispensable for invasion of macaque RBCs, and PkDBPα is sufficient to retain full growth rate in macaque cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that parasites with only PkDBPα maintain full growth in macaque RBCs.

claim: The PvDBPOR/Δ14Δγ line showed a 40% reduction in macaque multiplication rates compared to the PkDBPαOR/Δ14Δγ line.
source: Unlike P. knowlesi, P. vivax is unable to infect macaques, and sequence differences between the DARC receptor in the two hosts have been suggested to underlie this restriction (Tachibana et al., 2015). Whilst in macaque RBCs the multiplication rates and host preference ratio (1.16) were unaffected for the PvDBPOR/Δ14 line, the additional deletion of DBPγ in the PvDBPOR/Δ14Δγ line resulted in a 40% reduction in macaque multiplication rates (Figure 4B) which caused a shift to human RBC preference with a ratio of 0.75.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The PvDBPOR/Δ14Δγ line shifted to human RBC preference with a host preference ratio of 0.75.
source: Whilst in macaque RBCs the multiplication rates and host preference ratio (1.16) were unaffected for the PvDBPOR/Δ14 line, the additional deletion of DBPγ in the PvDBPOR/Δ14Δγ line resulted in a 40% reduction in macaque multiplication rates (Figure 4B) which caused a shift to human RBC preference with a ratio of 0.75.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and calculation of the host preference ratio.

claim: PvDBP is less effective at facilitating invasion of macaque cells than of human cells in the absence of redundant DBP pathways.
source: This suggests that in the absence of redundant DBP pathways, PvDBP is less effective at facilitating invasion of macaque cells than of human cells, but nevertheless can support invasion of both host cell types.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing reduced growth in macaque cells for the PvDBPOR/Δ14Δγ line.

claim: PvDBP can support invasion of both human and macaque host cell types.
source: This suggests that in the absence of redundant DBP pathways, PvDBP is less effective at facilitating invasion of macaque cells than of human cells, but nevertheless can support invasion of both host cell types.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that PvDBP-expressing parasites can invade both cell types.

claim: The Fy null phenotype protects individuals from P. vivax/P. knowlesi infection.
source: The Duffy gene exists as three distinct alleles, Fya, Fyb and Fynull. Whilst the Fy null phenotype has long been established to protect individuals from P. vivax/P. knowlesi infection (Miller et al., 1975; Miller et al., 1976), previous studies have also shown stronger binding of recombinant PvDBPRII to Fy(a−b+) and Fy(a+b+) human RBCs compared to Fy(a+b−) as well as higher risks of clinical episodes of P. vivax malaria in Fy(a−b+).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Miller et al., 1975 and Miller et al., 1976.

claim: Recombinant PvDBPRII shows stronger binding to Fy(a−b+) and Fy(a+b+) human RBCs compared to Fy(a+b−).
source: Whilst the Fy null phenotype has long been established to protect individuals from P. vivax/P. knowlesi infection (Miller et al., 1975; Miller et al., 1976), previous studies have also shown stronger binding of recombinant PvDBPRII to Fy(a−b+) and Fy(a+b+) human RBCs compared to Fy(a+b−) as well as higher risks of clinical episodes of P. vivax malaria in Fy(a−b+).
evidence: The claim is stated as previous findings from other studies.

claim: P. vivax may invade Fy(a+b−) RBCs less efficiently than other Duffy subtypes.
source: This suggests that P. vivax may invade to Fy(a+b−) RBCs less efficiently (King et al., 2011; Fong et al., 2018; Kano et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to King et al., 2011; Fong et al., 2018; Kano et al., 2018.

claim: No significant association was observed between growth of the PvDBPOR/Δ14Δγ line and Duffy haplotype.
source: Here, we also did not observe a significant association between growth of the PvDBPOR/Δ14Δγ line and Duffy haplotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: For all three parasite lines (wild type, PkDBPαOR/Δ14Δγ, and PvDBPOR/Δ14Δγ), the average growth rates in each of the three Fy subtypes were similar with no significant difference between growth in Fya and Fyb RBCs.
source: For all three lines the average growth rates in each of the three Fy subtypes were similar and there was no significant difference between growth in Fya and Fyb RBCs (Figure 4E–G; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4E-G.

claim: All parasite lines remained equally susceptible to invasion inhibition by anti-DARC camelid nanobody CA111 and polyclonal αPkMSP119 antibody.
source: Growth inhibition activity (GIA) assays revealed that all lines remained equally susceptible to invasion inhibition by both an anti-DARC camelid nanobody CA111 and a polyclonal αPkMSP119 antibody (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Purified IgGs from polyclonal rabbit sera raised against PvDBP_RII demonstrated low-level GIA activity (~30% inhibition at 10 mg/ml) for wild type and PkDBPαOR/ΔβΔγ lines.
source: In contrast, purified IgGs from polyclonal rabbit sera raised against PvDBP_RII, demonstrated low-level GIA activity for wild type and PkDBPaOR/ΔβΔγ lines (~30% inhibition at 10 mg/ml) but a significantly stronger GIA activity against the PvDBPOR/Δ14 and PvDBPOR/ΔβΔγ lines, reaching a maximum inhibition of ~75% at 10 mg/ml and around 50% at 4 mg/ml (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5B and C.

claim: Purified IgGs from polyclonal rabbit sera raised against PvDBP_RII demonstrated significantly stronger GIA activity against the PvDBPOR/Δ14 and PvDBPOR/ΔβΔγ lines, reaching a maximum inhibition of ~75% at 10 mg/ml.
source: In contrast, purified IgGs from polyclonal rabbit sera raised against PvDBP_RII, demonstrated low-level GIA activity for wild type and PkDBPaOR/ΔβΔγ lines (~30% inhibition at 10 mg/ml) but a significantly stronger GIA activity against the PvDBPOR/Δ14 and PvDBPOR/ΔβΔγ lines, reaching a maximum inhibition of ~75% at 10 mg/ml and around 50% at 4 mg/ml (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5B and C.

claim: At 2.5 mg/ml IgG, the GIA activity against the PvDBPOR/Δ14 and PvDBPOR/ΔβΔγ lines were 29.6 ± 3.3% and 24.6 ± 2.6%, significantly higher compared to wild type and PkDBPαOR/ΔβΔγ lines (p<0.001).
source: At 2.5 mg/ml IgG the GIA activity against the PvDBP OR/Δ14 and PvDBPOR/ΔβΔγ lines were 29.6 ± 3.3 and 24.6 ± 2.6% and significantly higher compared to wild type and PkDBPaOR/ΔβΔγ lines (p<0.001) (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5D and E.

claim: The PvDBPOR parasite lines could be readily inhibited by antibodies against the P. vivax protein.
source: The PvDBPOR parasite lines could thus be readily inhibited by antibodies against the P. vivax protein and the PkDBPα orthologues PkDBPγ and β appeared to play no interactive role.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the GIA assay results.

claim: The PkDBPα orthologues PkDBPγ and β appeared to play no interactive role in antibody-mediated growth inhibition.
source: The PvDBPOR parasite lines could thus be readily inhibited by antibodies against the P. vivax protein and the PkDBPα orthologues PkDBPγ and β appeared to play no interactive role.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that deletion of these genes did not affect antibody inhibition patterns.

claim: Targeting of the p230p locus demonstrated successful editing for 25/25 transfections.
source: Here we investigate key parameters associated with successful genome editing and show that the process is also highly robust; targeting of the p230p locus demonstrated successful editing for 25/25 transfections and only 1/10 sgRNAs targeting different loci failed to generate an edited line.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Only 1/10 sgRNAs targeting different loci failed to generate an edited line.
source: Here we investigate key parameters associated with successful genome editing and show that the process is also highly robust; targeting of the p230p locus demonstrated successful editing for 25/25 transfections and only 1/10 sgRNAs targeting different loci failed to generate an edited line.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: No off-target effects were detected in this study, consistent with other reports of CRISPR-Cas9 use in malaria parasites.
source: We did not detect any off-target effects, consistent with other reports of CRISPR-Cas9 use in malaria parasites (Ghorbal et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2016; Wagner et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study and citations to similar findings in other studies.

claim: Each round of genome editing requires only ~30 days including dilution cloning.
source: Negative selection of the pCas9/sg plasmid then enables generation of markerless lines allowing unlimited iterative modifications of the genome, with each round requiring only ~30 days (including dilution cloning).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from the study.

claim: The largest PCR construct generated was 6.1 kb in length (2 × 1.6 kb HRs flanking the 2.9 kb eGFP expression cassette).
source: The largest construct generated in this way was 6.1 kb in length (2 × 1.6 kb HRs flanking the 2.9 kb eGFP expression cassette).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Attempts to generate a larger 9.3 kb construct (2 × 3.2 kb HRs) failed during the final PCR step.
source: Attempts to generate a larger 9.3 kb construct (2 × 3.2 kb HRs) failed during the final PCR step.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from the study.

claim: Even human culture-adapted P. knowlesi retains a strong preference for macaque cells.
source: Even human culture-adapted P. knowlesi retains a strong preference for macaque cells (Moon et al., 2013; Lim et al., 2013; Moon et al., 2016) and it has been hypothesized that the additional invasion pathways provided by DBPβ and DBPγ are in part responsible for the increased invasion efficiency in macaque RBCs (Dankwa et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Moon et al., 2013; Lim et al., 2013; Moon et al., 2016.

claim: It has been hypothesized that the additional invasion pathways provided by DBPβ and DBPγ are in part responsible for the increased invasion efficiency in macaque RBCs.
source: Even human culture-adapted P. knowlesi retains a strong preference for macaque cells (Moon et al., 2013; Lim et al., 2013; Moon et al., 2016) and it has been hypothesized that the additional invasion pathways provided by DBPβ and DBPγ are in part responsible for the increased invasion efficiency in macaque RBCs (Dankwa et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dankwa et al., 2016.

claim: PkDBPα is the preferred and more efficient pathway for invasion in macaque cells even when DBPγ and DBPβ are functional.
source: The increased growth rate in macaque cells, would suggest that even here, where DBPγ and DBPβ are functional, PkDBPα is the preferred and more efficient pathway for invasion in macaque cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that deletion of DBPγ and DBPβ increases growth in macaque cells.

claim: Loss of DBPγ and DBPβ could provide an adaptation route to increased growth/virulence within human infections.
source: Importantly, this data suggests that loss of DBPγ and DBPβ could provide an adaptation route to increased growth/virulence within human infections.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation from the experimental findings.

claim: To achieve increased growth/virulence in humans through loss of DBPγ and DBPβ, parasites would need to sacrifice redundancy within their primary macaque hosts.
source: However, to do so the parasites would need to sacrifice redundancy within its primary macaque hosts – a situation only likely to occur with prolonged human to human transmission.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about evolutionary trade-offs.

claim: P. vivax cannot infect macaques despite being closely related to P. knowlesi and other macaque infecting species.
source: Despite being closely related to P. knowlesi and other macaque infecting species such as P. cynomolgi, P. vivax cannot infect macaques and the PvDBP protein has been suggested to play a role in enforcing this tropism, as key interacting residues are missing within the macaque DARC protein (Tachibana et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to Tachibana et al., 2015.

claim: Key interacting residues are missing within the macaque DARC protein, which has been suggested to enforce P. vivax tropism.
source: Despite being closely related to P. knowlesi and other macaque infecting species such as P. cynomolgi, P. vivax cannot infect macaques and the PvDBP protein has been suggested to play a role in enforcing this tropism, as key interacting residues are missing within the macaque DARC protein (Tachibana et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tachibana et al., 2015.

claim: The PvDBP protein alone is unlikely to represent a significant barrier to P. vivax infection of macaques.
source: P. knowlesi parasites expressing PvDBP in the absence of DBP paralogues demonstrate a significant reduction in growth in macaque cells, resulting in an overall shift towards preference for human cells consistent with PvDBP binding macaque DARC less efficiently. Nevertheless as the multiplication rate remained quite close to that seen for human RBCs it seems unlikely that the PvDBP protein alone represents a significant barrier to P. vivax infection of macaques.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that PvDBP-expressing parasites can still grow reasonably well in macaque cells.

claim: Recombinant PvDBP_RII binds 50% less efficiently to Fya RBCs compared to Fyb RBCs.
source: Previous work has shown that PvDBP_RII binds more strongly to RBCs expressing the Fyb allele of the Duffy antigen than Fya, with studies using recombinant protein demonstrating that the binding efficiency is 50% lower for Fya (Kano et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kano et al., 2018.

claim: The FyA phenotype is associated with a 30–80% reduced risk of clinical vivax malaria.
source: This effect was shown to correlate with a 30–80% reduced risk of clinical vivax malaria amongst patients with the FyA phenotype (King et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to King et al., 2011.

claim: The invasion process is very tolerant of even quite large changes in receptor-ligand affinity.
source: Whilst the size of our dataset cannot rule out relatively subtle effects on parasite growth rate, which over the course of an infection could become clinically relevant, it does rule out major growth differences and demonstrates that the invasion process is very tolerant of even quite large changes in receptor-ligand affinity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing no significant growth differences between Duffy subtypes.

claim: Fya+ RBCs demonstrate increased sensitivity to invasion-blocking antibodies.
source: Notably, the study first identifying a role for Duffy polymorphisms in P. vivax clinical susceptibility also demonstrated that the Fya+ RBCs demonstrate increased sensitivity to invasion-blocking antibodies, so protective effects may stem from this rather than a direct effect on invasion efficiency (King et al., 2011; Moon et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to King et al., 2011 and Moon et al., 2013.

claim: P. vivax has a strict restriction to invasion of reticulocytes unlike P. knowlesi.
source: Another key difference between the two species is that unlike P. knowlesi, P. vivax has a strict restriction to invasion of reticulocytes.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about the biology of these parasites.

claim: The reticulocyte binding-like proteins (RBPs) have been implicated in P. vivax reticulocyte tropism.
source: A second family of RBC binding proteins, known as the reticulocyte binding-like proteins (RBPs) have previously been implicated in this tropism.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge from previous research.

claim: DARC is present on both reticulocytes and mature normocytes but is only accessible to PvDBP binding in young reticulocytes according to work using recombinant PvDBP_RII.
source: More recently, the PvDBP protein itself has been implicated with work using recombinant PvDBP_RII suggesting that whilst DARC is present on both reticulocytes and mature normocytes, changes during red cell maturation mean that DARC is only accessible to PvDBP binding in young reticulocytes (Ovchynnikova et al., 2017; Haynes et al., 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ovchynnikova et al., 2017 and Haynes et al., 1988.

claim: Transgenic P. knowlesi parasites using PvDBP for invasion have no restriction to reticulocytes, invading human RBCs with the same efficiency as those expressing PkDBPα.
source: Here we show that transgenic P. knowlesi parasites using PvDBP for invasion have no such restriction, invading human RBCs (which typically contain less than 0.5% reticulocytes) with the same efficiency as those expressing PkDBPα – thus providing compelling evidence that PvDBP plays no role in the reticulocyte tropism.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: PvRBP2b binds to the reticulocyte specific marker CD71.
source: Further, recent work determining that PvRBP2b, which lacks an orthologue in P. knowlesi, binds to the reticulocyte specific marker CD71 further asserts the RBPs as the key to reticulocyte tropism.
evidence: The claim represents recent findings from other research.

claim: The RBPs are the key to reticulocyte tropism in P. vivax.
source: Further, recent work determining that PvRBP2b, which lacks an orthologue in P. knowlesi, binds to the reticulocyte specific marker CD71 further asserts the RBPs as the key to reticulocyte tropism.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from recent findings about PvRBP2b and the experimental data showing PvDBP does not restrict invasion to reticulocytes.

claim: There is a strong correlative link between activity in the in vitro GIA assay and in vivo protection from malaria challenge.
source: Whilst the relationship between in vitro GIA and in vivo protection against malaria challenge has not always been clear, previous studies have shown that there is a strong correlative link between activity in the in vitro assay of GIA and in vivo protection from challenge of two different species of human malaria (P. falciparum and P. knowlesi) in two different non-human primate models (Aotus monkeys and rhesus macaques) targeting three different merozoite proteins (PfAMA1, PfRH5, PfMSP1) (Douglas et al., 2015; Mahdi Abdel Hamid et al., 2011; Singh et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Douglas et al., 2015; Mahdi Abdel Hamid et al., 2011; Singh et al., 2006.

claim: A threshold value for in vitro GIA assay has been determined which must be reached before protection from malaria challenge is afforded.
source: Importantly, Douglas et al. in 2015 determined a threshold value for in vitro GIA assay which must be reached before protection from malaria challenge is afforded (Douglas et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Douglas et al., 2015.

claim: Cross-reactivity of PvDBP_RII antibodies against P. knowlesi suggests cross-immunity between the two species could exist in the field.
source: Our work also revealed low-level cross-reactivity of PvDBP_RII antibodies against P. knowlesi and suggests cross-immunity between the two species could exist in the field, which may have a significant impact on disease outcome.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observation of low-level cross-reactivity.
